title: Are the angles that face each other always equal?
description: Two lines cross with one angle of thirty five degrees. Two linear pairs give the angles b and d, and the same steps with a letter show that they are equal for any angle. Keeko doubts that the result holds only for thirty five degrees.
teaching_notes: One idea: b and d are each 180 take away a, so they are equal whatever a is; reasoning with a letter proves it for every crossing. Watch for students who think the rule is proved by measuring one crossing.

source: Two lines cross and a = 35°. Use linear pairs to find b and d, then show that they are equal for any value of a.
video_script.why: The child moves from one measured crossing to a reason that holds for every crossing.
video_script.substitution: The book's own argument for the crossing of two lines: each of b and d is a straight angle take away eigh, with eigh first a number and then any value.
video_script.anchor: Two lines crossing, with the four angles named a, b, c and d going round the crossing and a marked 35°.
video_script.wrong_answer: it works only for thirty five degrees
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks the result is proved for every angle by the one angle that was used.
video_script.payoff_line: Angles b and d are both one hundred and forty five degrees, and facing angles are always equal.

final_answer.value: b = 145°, d = 145°, vertically opposite angles are always equal
final_answer.spoken: angles b and d are both one hundred and forty five degrees, and vertically opposite angles are always equal

hold_back: b = 145°, d = 145°, vertically opposite angles are always equal
maths_rules: for any a: b = 180 - a and d = 180 - a, so b = d
the slip: one crossing with a = 35 is only one case
video_script.design: One crossing stays on the stage. First the number thirty five is used, then the same steps are shown with the letter a so the number can be wiped and replaced.

beats.on_screen: the small title card From your book appears; two lines cross; the four angles are named a, b, c and d going round the crossing, and a is 35°

marks.m1: the small title card From your book appears and two lines cross
marks.m2: the four angles are named a, b, c and d going round
marks.m3: b and d light up and a question mark appears

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book about two lines that cross.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The four angles are named eigh, b, c and d going round the crossing.
<bookmark mark='m2b'/>The angle eigh is thirty five degrees.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>If eigh were a different angle, would b and d still be equal?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: neighbouring angles lie along a straight line of 180°; neighbours are named a linear pair; angles facing each other are named vertically opposite angles

marks.m1: two neighbouring angles lie along a straight line of 180° and are named a linear pair
marks.m2: the angles b and d light up in one colour
marks.m3: they are named vertically opposite angles

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Neighbouring angles on a straight line are called a linear pair. They add up to one hundred and eighty degrees.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Angles that face each other across the crossing are called vertically opposite angles.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The angles b and d are one such pair.

beats.on_screen: Given: two lines cross and a = 35°

marks.m1: the given angle is written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, two lines cross and the angle eigh is thirty five degrees.

beats.on_screen: To find: b and d, and to show they are equal for any a

marks.m1: the words to find are written under the given

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find b and d. Then we show that they are equal for any value of eigh.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: a + b = 180 (linear pair), so b = 180 - 35 = 145

marks.m1: the pair a and b lights up on the line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one. The angles eigh and b are a linear pair, so they add up to one hundred and eighty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Then b is one hundred and eighty take away thirty five, which is one hundred and forty five.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: a + d = 180 (linear pair), so d = 180 - 35 = 145

marks.m1: the pair a and d lights up on the other line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two. The angles eigh and d are also a linear pair. They add up to one hundred and eighty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Then d is one hundred and eighty take away thirty five, which is one hundred and forty five.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: for any a, b = 180 - a and d = 180 - a, so b = d

marks.m1: the number 35 is wiped and the letter a stays
marks.m2: b = 180 - a and d = 180 - a are written one under the other

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three. Leave the number out and keep the letter eigh, whatever its size.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Both b and d are one hundred and eighty take away eigh. Then b and d are equal for every value of eigh.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: b + c = 180, so c = 180 - b = a

marks.m1: the pair b and c lights up on the line
marks.m2: c = 180 - b = a is written, and a and c light up in one colour

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four. In the same way, b and c are a linear pair. Then c is one hundred and eighty take away b.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>That is the same as eigh, so eigh and c are equal too.

beats.on_screen: Answer: b = 145°, d = 145°, vertically opposite angles are always equal

marks.m1: the answer is written and boxed
marks.m2: the word proof is written beside the argument

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Angles b and d are both one hundred and forty five degrees, and facing angles are always equal.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>A reason that works for every angle is called a proof.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the crossing
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble says the result is for 35° only; a new crossing with a different angle is drawn and the same two steps are written with the letter a

marks.m1: the bubble with the wrong idea appears
marks.m2: a new crossing with a different angle is drawn
marks.m3: the steps with the letter a replace the number

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks it works only for thirty five degrees, because that is the angle we used.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But one crossing is only one case.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>A rule must work for every angle. We reasoned with the letter eigh, not with one number.
